## Original files

All six are FLAC, 48 kHz, 24-bit, mono, recorded by Joseph SARDIN on a Hermes Precisa 305 portable manual typewriter with a Neumann KM184 into a Sound Devices MixPre-3 (as listed on each page). No account or login is needed to download them.

## How each file was made

Every pack file comes from exactly one of the downloads above, except the three `enter-bell-*` files, which mix two passages of one take. Processing, in order:

1. The FLAC is decoded exactly (24-bit integers to float, no resampling: the sources are already 48 kHz mono).
2. A 25 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth high-pass is applied to the whole recording (removes DC and rumble).
3. The passage listed below is cut out: it starts 0.5 ms before the onset (faded in over that 0.5 ms with a raised cosine) and ends with a raised-cosine fade-out ending on an exact zero (20 ms; 40 ms for Enter). For a type-bar strike the onset is the strike itself (the quiet key travel before it is not kept, so the sound starts without delay); the cut ends before the next sound in the take, or where the tail reaches the noise floor, or after 420 ms.
4. One gain per group (listed below), so the differences between strokes are kept.
5. Written as 16-bit PCM WAV, 48 kHz, mono. No compression, EQ, normalization, pitch or time changes.

Gains: type-bar strikes -5.34 dB (median strike peak -6 dBFS); take space strokes +9.67 dB and the single space shot -8.11 dB (median loudness 8 dB below the strikes); shift thuds +0.25 dB (9 dB below); Enter +6.66 dB (5 dB below). Loudness is the loudest 50 ms RMS. On the machine these sounds are much softer than a type bar hitting the platen; the offsets keep that order and make them audible.

Selection: the four takes contain 401 type-bar strikes; 149 are cleanly isolated (rejections: another key inside the stroke's own 175 ms 132; inside a bell or carriage-return region 7; next to an edit in the take 5; previous sound still ringing 1; previous strike < 180 ms before 22; shorter than 190 ms before the next sound 78; tail not decayed where the next sound starts 7). The least typical 15% were dropped and 40 mutually different strokes chosen from the rest, by spectrum and level. 14 space-bar strokes in the takes matched the single space shot; 10 were chosen the same way. The 4 shift pairs are every capital letter in the takes with a clean thud before and after it. Releases: only the modifiers have release sounds, because only the shift's release is a separate sound in the recordings (a thud 0.2-0.25 s after the capital, when the basket drops back). A type bar's return and escapement clicks follow its strike by about 0.1 s and stay in the press sound; none is cut out as a release.

## Loudness

`volume` in `pack.json` is 1.29 (+2.2 dB): a playback gain the app applies to the whole pack, so no audio file changes. Typing loudness is matched across the bundled packs so that switching packs does not jump in volume; the target is TakTak's reference typing level, -25.8 LK. Measured with `cargo run -p synth-packs --release -- loudness packs/typewriter` (`tools/synth-packs/src/loudness.rs`): the K-weighted (ITU-R BS.1770) energy of the first 100 ms of the sample each alphanumeric key plays on press by default, power-averaged over the keys, on the samples as the app loads them at 48 kHz. The pack reads -28.4 LK as built, so the reference would take a volume of 1.35. Headroom caps it at 1.29: the loudest file's true peak (-3.77 dBFS, 4x oversampled) must stay at or below -1 dBFS at the top of the +-6% volume variation, because the mixer clips hard at 0 dBFS (it reaches -1.05 dBFS). Typing plays at -26.2 LK, 0.4 dB below the reference (within the 0.5 dB tolerance). `build.py` writes the volume (`VOLUME`), so a rebuild keeps it.

## Key mapping

- `alphanumeric`: the type-bar strikes (`key-*`): each key keeps one of them (with random variants on, one is picked at random per keystroke). Other keys without a group of their own (arrows, function keys, ...) fall back to them.
- `space`: the space-bar strokes (`space-*`). `backspace` uses them too: a manual typewriter's backspace moves the carriage like the space bar and has no type bar.
- `modifiers`: `shift-down-*` on press and `shift-up-*` on release.
- `enter`: six carriage returns (`enter-return-*`) and three that ring the margin bell first (`enter-bell-*`). Each Enter key keeps one of them: Enter plays `enter-bell-2`, so it rings the bell every time, and NumpadEnter plays `enter-return-5`, a plain return (with random variants on, both pick one of the nine at random per keystroke, and about one return in three rings the bell).

## Not used

Downloaded for this pack on 2026-10-02 (CC0) but not used:

- BigSoundBank 2835-2837 "Typewriter #2-#4" (same author, machine and license): stereo files whose channels are only weakly correlated (0.03-0.2) and offset by up to 0.5 ms, so a mono fold-down would comb-filter; their strokes are also brighter than the mono takes'. The mono takes have more than enough strokes.
- BigSoundBank 2844 and 2845 "Typewriter, Bell": stand-alone bell rings, 2.4-2.6 s long and leveled on their own (peaks at 0 dBFS). The margin bells inside the takes are used instead: each comes with the carriage return the typist made after it, at the level it was recorded at.
- BigSoundBank 1065 "Typewriter #1": a different recording setup (Tascam DR-40 and Sennheiser ME66, 16-bit) and typewriter model not stated.
- OpenGameArt "Typewriter sounds" by Cassie-OrbitGames (typewriter1-8.wav, https://opengameart.org/content/typewriter-sounds, CC0, checked 2026-10-02): phone recordings of an unnamed typewriter at 22.05 kHz (nothing above 11 kHz; 7 of the 8 files are stereo). Each 0.28-0.69 s clip holds 6-14 separate mechanical events, and the loudest strike in each is preceded by 60-160 ms of other mechanism sounds, so no cut gives a clean stroke that starts on its strike. Picked at random next to the 48 kHz studio strikes above, they would also sound like a second, duller machine. Because nothing from them is used, `pack.json` credits only Joseph Sardin.
